content: Soybean wax, commonly referred to as soy wax, is derived from hydrogenated soybean oil. It was invented in 1993 by Michael Richards, who sought a more cost-effective alternative to beeswax. This innovation marked the first significant advancement in candle wax technology in over a century. One of the primary drawbacks of soybean wax is its relatively low melting point. This characteristic makes candles made from soy wax prone to deformation in hot weather and causes them to drip more readily when burned. There is no documented evidence to suggest that soy wax is a safer alternative to paraffin wax. However, it is often less expensive than beeswax. Due to the chemical additives required to transform soybeans into a usable wax, its biodegradability is generally considered comparable to that of paraffin and beeswax. Soy is classified as a major food allergen by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). For individuals who experience allergic reactions to soy, paraffin wax may serve as a safer alternative.
